title: Part 6, Chapter 4
paragraphs: "You know, perhaps — yes, I told you myself," Svidrigailov began, "that I was in debtors' prison here, for a huge sum, with no prospect of paying it off. There's no need to go into how Marfa Petrovna bought my freedom. Do you know to what insane lengths a woman can sometimes love? She was an honest woman, and very sensible, though completely uneducated. But would you believe that this honest, jealous woman, after many hysterical scenes and reproaches, agreed to enter into a kind of contract with me — one she kept throughout our entire marriage? She was considerably older than me, and besides, she always had a clove or something in her mouth. There was enough swine in my soul — and enough honesty too, of a sort — to tell her straight out that I couldn't be absolutely faithful. This confession drove her into a frenzy, but she seems to have almost liked my brutal frankness. She thought it showed I was unwilling to deceive her by warning her in advance, and for a jealous woman, that's the main thing. After many tears, an unwritten contract was drawn up between us: first, I would never leave Marfa Petrovna and would always be her husband; second, I would never go anywhere without her permission; third, I would never take a permanent mistress; fourth, in return, Marfa Petrovna gave me free rein with the servant girls, but only with her secret knowledge; fifth, God forbid I fall in love with a woman of our own class; sixth, if I were ever visited by a great, serious passion — God forbid — I was obligated to reveal it to Marfa Petrovna. On this last point, however, Marfa Petrovna was fairly relaxed. She was sensible enough, and she couldn't help seeing me as a dissolute wastrel incapable of real love. But a sensible woman and a jealous woman are two very different things, and that's where the trouble came in. To judge some people fairly, though, we have to abandon certain preconceptions and our habitual attitudes toward ordinary people. I have more reason to trust your judgment than anyone's. Perhaps you've already heard plenty that was ridiculous and absurd about Marfa Petrovna. She certainly had some very ridiculous ways, but I tell you frankly: I feel genuine regret for the countless griefs I caused her. Well, I think that's enough by way of a decent funeral oration for the most tender wife of a most tender husband. When we quarreled, I usually held my tongue and didn't provoke her — and that gentlemanly restraint rarely failed. It influenced her, even pleased her; there were times she was positively proud of me. But your sister she could never abide. How she ever risked taking such a beautiful creature into her house as a governess — I can only explain it by saying that Marfa Petrovna was a passionate, impressionable woman who simply fell in love with your sister. Well, who could blame her — look at Avdotya Romanovna! I saw the danger at first glance, and — what do you think? — I resolved not to even look at her. But Avdotya Romanovna herself took the first step — would you believe it? And would you believe that Marfa Petrovna was actually angry with me at first for my stubborn silence about your sister, for my indifferent reception of her endless adoring praise of Avdotya Romanovna? I don't know what she wanted! Of course, Marfa Petrovna told Avdotya Romanovna every detail about me. She had that unfortunate habit of telling literally everyone all our family secrets and constantly complaining about me; how could she not confide in such a wonderful new friend? I expect they talked about nothing else but me, and no doubt Avdotya Romanovna heard all the dark, mysterious rumors about me... I don't mind betting you've heard some of them too?"
"I have. Luzhin accused you of causing the death of a child. Is that true?"
"Please don't bring up those vulgar stories," Svidrigailov said with disgust and irritation. "If you absolutely insist on hearing about all that foolishness, I'll tell you one day, but now..."
"I also heard about some servant of yours in the country whom you mistreated."
"I beg you to drop the subject," Svidrigailov interrupted again with obvious impatience.
"Was that the servant who came to you after death to fill your pipe?... You told me about it yourself." Raskolnikov was growing more and more irritated.
Svidrigailov looked at him closely, and Raskolnikov thought he caught a flash of malicious mockery in that look. But Svidrigailov restrained himself and answered quite civilly:

"Yes, it was. I can see you're extremely curious about all this, and I'll consider it my duty to satisfy your curiosity at the first opportunity. My God — I see I really could pass for a romantic figure with some people. Judge how grateful I must be to Marfa Petrovna for telling Avdotya Romanovna all that mysterious, interesting gossip about me. I can only guess what impression it made, but in any case it worked in my favor. Despite Avdotya Romanovna's natural aversion, and despite my invariably dark and repellent manner — she did come to pity me, pity a lost soul. And once a girl's heart is moved to pity, it's more dangerous than anything. She's bound to want to 'save him,' to bring him to his senses, lift him up, redirect him to nobler aims, restore him to new life and usefulness — well, we all know how far such dreams can go. I saw at once that the bird was flying into the cage on its own. And I prepared accordingly. You're frowning, Rodion Romanovitch? No need. As you know, it all ended in nothing. (Damn, I'm drinking a lot!) You know, I always regretted, from the very beginning, that fate didn't arrange for your sister to be born in the second or third century A.D. as the daughter of a reigning prince or some governor in Asia Minor. She would undoubtedly have been one of those who endured martyrdom with a smile as hot pincers seared her breast. She would have gone to it willingly. And in the fourth or fifth century, she'd have walked off into the Egyptian desert to live for thirty years on roots and ecstasies and visions. She's simply burning to endure some torment for someone, and if she can't find her torment, she'll throw herself out a window. I've heard something about a Mr. Razumikhin — they say he's a sensible fellow; his surname suggests it. He's probably a theology student. Well, he'd better look after your sister! I like to think I understand her, and I'm proud of it. But at the beginning of an acquaintance, as you know, one tends to be more careless and stupid. You don't see clearly. Damn it all — why is she so beautiful? It's not my fault. In short, it began on my side with an irresistible physical desire. Avdotya Romanovna is extraordinarily chaste — incredibly, phenomenally so. Take note: I'm telling you this about your sister as a fact. She is almost morbidly chaste, despite her broad intelligence, and it will stand in her way. There was a girl in the house then, Parasha, a dark-eyed wench I'd never seen before — she'd just arrived from another village — very pretty but incredibly stupid. She burst into tears, wailed so loudly the whole house could hear, and caused a scandal. One day after dinner, Avdotya Romanovna followed me into a garden path and, with blazing eyes, insisted I leave poor Parasha alone. It was nearly our first private conversation. I was naturally delighted to comply, tried to appear flustered and embarrassed — played my part rather well, in short. Then came more meetings, private talks, pleas, entreaties, even tears — would you believe it, even tears? Think what the passion for moral reform can bring some young women to! I, of course, blamed everything on destiny, posed as a man hungering and thirsting for enlightenment, and finally deployed the most powerful weapon for the conquest of a woman's heart — one that never fails. It's the well-known technique: flattery. Nothing in the world is harder than speaking the truth, and nothing easier than flattery. If there's even the slightest false note in speaking the truth, it creates discord, and discord means trouble. But if flattery is false from first note to last, it's still perfectly agreeable, and heard with genuine pleasure. However crude the flattery, at least half of it will seem true. That holds for all levels of education and all classes of society. Even a vestal virgin could be seduced by flattery. I can never think without laughing of how I once seduced a lady devoted to her husband, her children, and her principles. What fun it was, and how little effort! And the lady really did have principles — of her own sort, anyway. My entire strategy consisted of appearing utterly demolished and prostrate before her purity. I flattered her shamelessly, and each time I managed to get a squeeze of the hand or a glance, I'd reproach myself for having stolen it by force, declaring she'd resisted and that I could never have gotten anywhere if I weren't so shameless. I insisted she was so innocent she couldn't have foreseen my treachery, and had yielded unconsciously, without realizing it. In a word, I triumphed, while the lady remained firmly convinced she was innocent, chaste, faithful to all her duties, and had fallen purely by accident. And how angry she was when I finally told her it was my sincere belief she'd been just as eager as I! Poor Marfa Petrovna was terribly susceptible to flattery too; if I'd wanted to, I could have had all her property signed over to me during her lifetime. (I'm drinking far too much wine and talking too much.) I hope you won't be angry if I mention that I was beginning to produce the same effect on Avdotya Romanovna. But I was stupid and impatient and ruined everything. Several times — one time in particular — Avdotya Romanovna was deeply displeased by the expression of my eyes. Would you believe it? There was sometimes a light in them that frightened her, growing stronger and more brazen until it became hateful to her. No need for details, but we parted. Then I did something stupid again. I began mocking all such reforming efforts and attempts to convert me in the crudest way; Parasha returned to the scene, and not just her — in short, there was a huge uproar. Ah, Rodion Romanovitch, if you could only see how your sister's eyes can flash sometimes! Never mind that I'm drunk and have had a whole glass of wine — I'm telling you the truth. I assure you, that look haunted my dreams; eventually even the rustle of her dress became more than I could stand. I honestly began to think I might become epileptic. I would never have believed I could be driven to such frenzy. A reconciliation was essential, but by then it was impossible. And imagine what I did! To what depths of stupidity frenzy can drive a man! Never attempt anything in a frenzy, Rodion Romanovitch. I calculated that Avdotya Romanovna was, after all, a pauper (forgive me — that's not the right word, but does it matter if it conveys the meaning?), that she lived by her work, that she had her mother and you to support (you're scowling again), and I decided to offer her all my money — thirty thousand rubles I could have raised at the time — if she'd run away with me to Petersburg. Of course I'd have sworn eternal love, rapture, and the rest. And you know, I was so wild about her that if she'd told me to poison Marfa Petrovna or slit her throat and then marry me — I'd have done it at once! But it ended in the disaster you already know about. You can imagine my fury when I learned Marfa Petrovna had gotten hold of that vile attorney Luzhin and practically arranged a match — which amounted to exactly the same thing I was proposing. Am I right? Am I? I notice you've begun listening very closely... interesting young man..."

Svidrigailov struck the table with his fist impatiently. He was flushed. Raskolnikov saw clearly that the glass or glass and a half of champagne he'd been sipping unconsciously was affecting him — and he decided to take advantage of the opportunity. He was deeply suspicious of Svidrigailov.
"Well, after everything you've said, I'm fully convinced you came to Petersburg with designs on my sister," he said directly, deliberately trying to provoke him.
"Oh, nonsense," Svidrigailov said, seeming to shake himself awake. "I told you... besides, your sister can't stand me."
"I'm certain she can't. But that's not the point."

"Are you so sure she can't?" Svidrigailov screwed up his eyes and smiled mockingly. "You're right — she doesn't love me. But you can never be sure what's passed between a husband and wife, or between a lover and his mistress. There's always a small corner that stays secret from the world, known only to the two people involved. Can you swear that Avdotya Romanovna looked at me with nothing but revulsion?"
"From certain things you've let slip, I gather you still have designs — evil ones, naturally — on Dunya, and that you intend to carry them out without delay."
"What, have I let things slip like that?" Svidrigailov asked in naive dismay, paying absolutely no attention to the word "evil" attached to his designs.
"You're letting them slip right now. Why are you so frightened? What are you so afraid of?"
"Me — afraid? Afraid of you? You're the one who should be afraid of me, cher ami. But what nonsense... I've drunk too much, I can see that. Nearly said too much again. Damn the wine! Hey — water!"
He grabbed the champagne bottle and flung it unceremoniously out the window. Philip brought water.
"That's all nonsense!" Svidrigailov said, wetting a towel and pressing it to his head. "But I can demolish all your suspicions with a single word. Did you know I'm getting married?"
"You told me that before."

"Did I? I've forgotten. But I couldn't have said so definitely, because I hadn't even met my bride then. I only had the idea. But now I actually have a fiancée, and it's all settled. If I didn't have business that can't wait, I'd take you to meet them right now, because I'd like to ask your advice. Oh damn — only ten minutes left! Look at the time. But I must tell you about my marriage — it's an interesting story in its own way. Where are you off to? Leaving again?"
"No, I'm not leaving now."

"Not at all? We'll see. I will take you there — I'll show you my bride — but not now. You'll need to go soon anyway. You'll go right, and I'll go left. Do you know Madame Resslich, the woman I'm lodging with? I know what you're thinking — she's the woman whose girl supposedly drowned herself last winter. Come, are you listening? She arranged the whole thing for me. 'You're bored,' she said, 'you need something to fill your time.' Because, you know, I'm a gloomy, depressive sort. You think I'm lighthearted? No — I'm gloomy. I do no harm, but I sit in a corner for three days without saying a word. And that Resslich is a sly one, I tell you. I know what she has in mind: she thinks I'll get tired of my wife, abandon her, and leave — and then she'll get hold of the girl and make a profit from her, among our class or higher. She told me the father was a broken-down retired official who's been sitting in a wheelchair for three years, paralyzed. The mother, she said, was a sensible woman. There's a son serving in the provinces who never helps, a married daughter who never visits. And they're raising two little nephews on top of their own children, as if they didn't have enough trouble. They pulled their youngest daughter out of school — a girl who'll be sixteen in another month — so she could be married off. She was meant for me. We went to see them. What a comedy! I present myself: a landowner, a widower, from a well-known family, with connections and a fortune. What does it matter that I'm fifty and she's not yet sixteen? Who cares about that? But it is fascinating, isn't it? It's fascinating, ha-ha! You should have seen me talking to the parents. It was priceless. She comes in, curtseys — you can imagine, still in a short dress — an unopened bud! Blushing like a sunset — they'd told her, no doubt. I don't know how you feel about female faces, but in my view, these sixteen years, these childish eyes, this shyness and these bashful tears are lovelier than beauty. And she's a perfect little picture too: fair hair in little curls like a lamb's, plump rosy lips, tiny feet — a charmer!... Well, we became friends. I told them I was in a hurry due to family circumstances, and the very next day — that is, the day before yesterday — we were engaged. Now whenever I visit, I take her on my knee right away and keep her there... She blushes like a sunset, and I kiss her every minute. Her mother naturally impresses on her that this is her husband and this is how it must be. It's delicious! The current betrothed state may actually be better than marriage itself. Here you have what they call la nature et la vérité! Ha-ha! I've talked to her twice; she's far from stupid. Sometimes she sneaks a look at me that positively scorches. Her face is like Raphael's Madonna — you know, the Sistine Madonna has something fantastical in it, something of mournful religious ecstasy. Haven't you noticed? Well, she has something of that look. The day after the engagement, I bought her presents worth fifteen hundred rubles — a diamond set, a pearl set, and a silver dressing case as big as this, full of everything — and even my Madonna's face glowed. I sat her on my knee yesterday, a bit too freely I suppose — she turned crimson and tears appeared, but she tried not to show it. We were left alone, and she suddenly threw her arms around my neck — for the first time, of her own accord — kissed me, and vowed she would be an obedient, faithful, good wife, that she'd make me happy, devote every minute of her life to me, sacrifice everything, everything — and that all she wants in return is my respect, and that she wants 'nothing, nothing more from me — no presents.' You'll agree that to hear such a confession from a sixteen-year-old angel in a muslin dress, with curls and a blush of maidenly modesty and tears of rapture in her eyes — it's rather captivating, isn't it? It's something worth having, isn't it? Well... listen, let's go see my fiancée — only not right now!"
"The fact is, this monstrous difference in age and maturity excites your lust! Will you really go through with such a marriage?"

"Why not? Certainly. Everyone thinks of himself, and the man who's best at deceiving himself lives the most cheerfully. Ha-ha! But why this sudden passion for virtue? Have mercy on me, my friend. I'm a sinful man. Ha-ha-ha!"
"But you've made arrangements for Katerina Ivanovna's children. Though... you had your own reasons for that... I understand everything now."

"I'm very fond of children — always have been," Svidrigailov laughed. "I can tell you a curious example. My first day here, I visited various haunts — after seven years, I simply threw myself at them. You've probably noticed I'm in no rush to reconnect with old friends. I'll manage without them as long as I can. You know, when I was with Marfa Petrovna in the country, the thought of these places, where a man who knows his way around can find plenty, haunted me. Yes, upon my soul! The peasants have vodka, the educated young people shut out from activity waste themselves on impossible dreams and theories; Jews spring up and hoard money; everyone else gives themselves over to debauchery. From the first hour, the city reeked of its familiar smells. I happened into a ghastly den — I like my dens filthy — and there was a so-called dance, with a cancan the likes of which I'd never seen in my day. Yes, there's progress for you. Suddenly I noticed a girl of thirteen, nicely dressed, dancing with a specialist in that line, facing another partner. Her mother was sitting in a chair by the wall. You can't imagine what that cancan was like! The girl felt ashamed, blushed, and finally felt insulted and began to cry. Her partner grabbed her, started spinning her around and performing in front of her; everyone laughed — I like your public, even the cancan public — they laughed and shouted: 'Serves her right! That's what she gets for bringing children!' Well, it's not my concern whether that reasoning was logical or not. I immediately made my plan. I sat down beside the mother and explained that I too was a stranger, that people here were rude and couldn't recognize decent folk or treat them respectfully. I let her understand I had plenty of money, offered to take them home in my carriage. I took them home and got to know them. They were staying in a miserable little hole, having just arrived from the country. She told me she and her daughter could only regard my acquaintance as an honor. I learned they had nothing of their own and had come to the city on some legal matter. I offered my services and money. I found out they'd gone to the dance hall by mistake, thinking it was a real dance school. I offered to help with the girl's education in French and dancing. The offer was accepted with enthusiasm as a great honor — and we're still on friendly terms... If you'd like, we'll go visit them — only not just now."
"Stop! Enough of your vile, disgusting stories, you depraved, loathsome man!"
"Schiller! A true Schiller! O la vertu va-t-elle se nicher? But you know, I'm going to keep telling you these things on purpose, just for the pleasure of hearing your outrage!"
"Of course you are. I can see I'm making a fool of myself," Raskolnikov muttered angrily.
Svidrigailov laughed heartily. Then he called Philip, paid his bill, and started getting up.
"Well, I'm drunk — assez causé," he said. "It's been a pleasure."

"I should think so!" cried Raskolnikov, also rising. "Naturally it's entertaining for a worn-out degenerate to describe such adventures — with some equally monstrous scheme already in mind — especially to a man like me and in circumstances like these... It's stimulating!"

"Well, if you put it that way," Svidrigailov replied, examining Raskolnikov with some surprise, "if you put it that way, you're quite a cynic yourself. You've got the raw material, at any rate. You can understand a great deal... and do a great deal too. But enough. I sincerely regret we haven't talked more, but I won't lose sight of you... Just wait a bit."

Svidrigailov walked out of the restaurant. Raskolnikov followed. Svidrigailov was not, in fact, very drunk — the wine had affected him briefly, but the effect was already passing. He was preoccupied with something important and clearly excited, anxious in anticipation of something. His manner toward Raskolnikov had been changing over the past few minutes, growing ruder and more sneering. Raskolnikov noticed all of this and was uneasy himself. He became deeply suspicious of Svidrigailov and decided to follow him.
They came out onto the sidewalk.
"You go to the right, and I to the left — or the other way around, if you prefer. Only — adieu, mon plaisir. May we meet again."
And he walked off to the right, toward the Hay Market.
